what_it_does: The most computationally expensive step in running a neural network is multiplying large rectangular tables of numbers together (called matrix multiplication or GEMM, for General Matrix Multiply). This paper observes that many intermediate results produced during such a multiplication can be reused to compute other results rather than being discarded and recomputed from scratch — the authors call this 'transitive sparsity,' a new form of skipping redundant work. The dependencies between which results can reuse which are encoded as a directed acyclic graph (essentially a family tree of calculations, with arrows showing which result feeds into which). A hardware accelerator called the Transitive Array is designed around this idea: instead of performing all multiplications independently, it routes previously computed partial results to where they are needed, eliminating a large fraction of multiplication operations entirely. Multiple computation lanes work in parallel to maintain throughput.
